text:
Samsung S21 & S22 models aren't the best years for Samsung.

Their S23 and S24 intl models are good now.

May mga lemon products naman talaga lahat ng companies and Apple is no exception.

Yung iPhone 12 is plagued with the same green line issues din and horrendous battery life, iPhone 11 had dead pixel issues as time goes on.

If u bought the iPhone 12 instead of the S22 back then, you'd say the same thing and say never using an iPhone and switching to Samsung na.

Best to do generally is to do market research muna before buying a tech product.

I never buy a tech product that is just newly released, I wait about 6 months to about 1 year because that's the time where people get problems with their products.

And besides, soon as the newly released tech gets into the market, discount prices rises up for clearance sales. So its a win-win.

text:
Oh my god.. i thought you asking for an app to download on your phone to be able to shoot almost professional videos on your phone.. Oh okay.. so the answer here is pretty clear.. It doesn't have anything to do with the number of Mega Pixels... When looking at the camera specs Mega Pixels have the least amount of impact of the quality, so just ignore that number. 
The most important thing is the size of the sensor. The bigger the better, obviously. S25 and iPhone 16/17 have the same size for their main sensor 1/1.56", but...  the numbers in specification sheet are not saying everything. They are telling the state of the hardware but phone is not just hardware. It should be near perfect integration and optimization with the software. 

iPhone and Android phones are very different but similar in results and it was always depending on our preference on which world we like more. But... iPhone was always better in that one area from its counterparts from Android world and that's shooting videos. 

Its because of their (near) perfect optimization the software with the hardware and because they are made for each other from the very start of designing the phone. author: @iamsid23
text:
@Sacto1654 Not much, actually. There's a misconception that 120Hz runs all the time, but that's not true. It only kicks in while scrolling, in games that need it, or in other areas where smoothness is required. When you watch a video or perform other tasks, it automatically adjusts to 60Hz or whatever framerate is needed to play the content. So, the percentage of time 120Hz is active is minimal, but it makes a huge difference in day-to-day use. That's also why the impact on battery life is minimal, though smartphones today require daily charging anyway.

author: @scr34m36
text:
Well, there's a lot of people talking about 60hz. Well here's my take on it:
Lately, I’ve found myself actually preferring 60Hz on the iPhone. Now, hear me out before hating on me.

I use both Android and iOS daily. My Android device runs on a Snapdragon 888, rocking a 120Hz AMOLED display, while my other go-to is the iPhone 15 Plus. On my Android, I’ve tweaked things like window animation, transition, and animator duration to 0.5x, while keeping the display locked at 120Hz refresh rate, which makes everything feel snappier and reduces input lag.

On the iPhone, though, I don’t have that kind of control because, well, iOS is locked down. But here’s what surprised me: the iPhone’s carefully tuned animations make its 60Hz feel just as smooth as 120Hz on Android, specifically the animation duration. And the bonus? It’s the reason my iPhone easily lasts 2+ days on moderate use, even with a charging cap of 80%.

Yet, Android remains my favorite because it lets me mold the experience how I want it. The openness of Android isn’t just a feature; it’s a whole vibe. Honestly, it’s the best mobile OS out there, no contest.

For me it’s like living with two personas: iPhone for the serious, task-driven side of me, and Android for everything else. Sure, there’s a list of things I prefer on Android, but iPhone does shine in certain areas too.

If Apple deserves backlash, it’s not for sticking with 60Hz displays but for their walled-garden approach, which doesn't let you actually "own" the device. They lock out the open-source community, barring the potential for innovation.

In the end, my dream device? Apple’s hardware, running Google’s Android. That would be the perfect fusion.

author: @LinkyLabs
text:
I got the base teal iPhone 16 128GB in January of 2025. It was simply the only option I could actually afford. It was my transition from Android to iPhone since a very long time, as well as a testing device to help me with application development.

It has been awesome so far. I can't stress how premium the phone is. The design is simply gorgeous, the camera quality is beautiful, the display, etc. It's simply an amazing phone all around, and the battery life is pretty decent too, but nothing too crazy of course. It's just very triggering for me that Apple just 1 year after made a phone with the same MSRP price with 120Hz and 256GB, both SIGNIFICANTLY improving the experience considering the price you pay. It's certainly disheartening how they stayed on 60Hz all this long for non-pro iPhones. I knew it was ought to change in the very near future, but I didn't think it would be THAT near lol. All in all, it’s still a great phone, but oh please if you see the iPhone 17 with a little price difference GET THAT THING! It's simply a significant improvement for base iPhones in battery life, refresh rate, and storage capacity!
